name: US-Japan trade tensions
initial_dynamic: Rising economic rivalry as Japanese manufacturing (autos, electronics) outcompeted US industry; US ran large trade deficits and accused Japan of unfair trade practices.
trajectory: Escalated through the 1980s (tariff threats, 'Japan bashing', VER agreements) but never became military or existentially hostile. Tensions eased through the 1990s as Japan's economy stagnated (the 'Lost Decade') and the relative threat diminished on its own.
outcome: De-escalated via managed trade agreements plus Japan's own economic slowdown, not via resolution of the underlying grievance. Alliance (security treaty) held throughout.
key_lesson: Economic rivalries between allies with deep security ties tend to stay contained below the threshold of real hostility, and can resolve simply because one side's relative power declines.

name: US-Soviet Cold War
initial_dynamic: Ideological and geopolitical rivalry between two nuclear superpowers after WWII, with proxy wars, an arms race, and no direct military conflict between the two.
trajectory: Multiple phases of extreme tension (Cuban Missile Crisis, early 1980s) alternating with detente (1970s arms control). Ended not through military defeat but through the Soviet Union's internal economic and political collapse.
outcome: Rivalry ended via one side's systemic collapse, not negotiated resolution. Took over 40 years.
key_lesson: Long-running great-power rivalries can persist for decades with no clear endpoint, and can end abruptly for internal reasons unrelated to the bilateral dynamic itself.

name: Anglo-German naval arms race
initial_dynamic: Germany's naval buildup under Tirpitz challenged British naval supremacy, seen by Britain as a direct threat given its dependence on sea power.
trajectory: Escalating shipbuilding competition (dreadnoughts) combined with alliance polarization (Triple Entente vs Triple Alliance) with no successful off-ramp attempted seriously enough.
outcome: Escalated into World War I. The arms race itself didn't cause the war but built the alliance blocs and mutual threat perception that made a regional crisis (Sarajevo) turn into a general war.
key_lesson: Unmanaged arms races between rising and established powers, layered on top of rigid alliance systems, are a classic escalation pattern — the triggering event is often unrelated to the underlying rivalry.

name: US-China rapprochement
initial_dynamic: Two decades of hostility (Korean War, no diplomatic relations) between the US and Communist China.
trajectory: Shared strategic interest in countering the Soviet Union drove secret diplomacy (Kissinger's 1971 visit), Nixon's 1972 visit, and eventual normalization in 1979.
outcome: Rapid improvement in relations driven almost entirely by a shared external threat (the USSR), not by resolution of underlying ideological differences.
key_lesson: A common adversary can flip a hostile relationship quickly, even without resolving the original source of hostility — but the relationship can be fragile once the shared threat disappears.

name: Franco-German reconciliation
initial_dynamic: Three wars in 70 years (1870, WWI, WWII) between historic rivals, deep mutual distrust after WWII.
trajectory: Deliberate institutional binding via the Coal and Steel Community (1951, making war 'materially impossible' by pooling the resources needed to fight one), followed by deeper economic integration and the 1963 Elysee Treaty.
outcome: Complete transformation from repeated existential enemies to the core partnership of European integration, within about 15-20 years of the last war.
key_lesson: Deliberate economic interdependence, designed specifically to make conflict costly, can durably transform even the deepest historical rivalries — but it required sustained political will on both sides, not just economic incentive.

name: India-Pakistan relations
initial_dynamic: Hostile partition in 1947 with immediate war over Kashmir; rivalry rooted in territorial dispute plus religious/national identity.
trajectory: Four wars (1947, 1965, 1971, 1999) and repeated crises, punctuated by brief periods of dialogue that have consistently broken down. Both became nuclear powers by 1998.
outcome: Unresolved after 75+ years; nuclearization has made full-scale war less likely but not eliminated periodic military crises.
key_lesson: Rivalries anchored in an unresolved territorial/identity dispute (not just interests) can persist indefinitely, and nuclear deterrence tends to cap escalation rather than resolve the underlying conflict.

name: North-South Korea division
initial_dynamic: Korean War (1950-53) ended in armistice, not a peace treaty, leaving the peninsula divided along the DMZ.
trajectory: Decades of frozen hostility with occasional flare-ups (naval clashes, artillery exchanges) and periodic diplomatic thaws (Sunshine Policy, 2018 summits) that failed to produce lasting change.
outcome: Technically still at war 70+ years later; no resolution despite multiple serious diplomatic attempts.
key_lesson: A conflict frozen by an armistice rather than resolved by treaty can remain stable-but-unresolved for generations, with diplomatic breakthroughs proving reversible rather than durable.

name: Israel-Egypt peace
initial_dynamic: Four wars between 1948 and 1973, existential hostility.
trajectory: After the costly 1973 war, Sadat made an unexpected diplomatic overture (1977 Jerusalem visit), leading to US-brokered Camp David Accords (1978) and a full peace treaty (1979).
outcome: Durable peace treaty that has held for 45+ years, despite continued regional tension elsewhere.
key_lesson: A costly near-miss war can create the political opening for a dramatic reversal, especially when a third party (the US) actively brokers and backs the deal with sustained incentives.

name: US-Iran relations
initial_dynamic: 1979 Islamic Revolution overthrew the US-backed Shah; hostage crisis destroyed diplomatic relations.
trajectory: 45+ years of hostility including sanctions, proxy conflicts, and occasional near-military confrontations, punctuated by one major diplomatic opening (2015 nuclear deal) that later collapsed (2018 US withdrawal).
outcome: Still unresolved; the one major breakthrough proved reversible when domestic politics in the US changed.
key_lesson: A relationship broken by a revolution/regime change can stay broken for generations, and negotiated breakthroughs are fragile if they depend on one government staying in power.

name: Sino-Soviet split
initial_dynamic: Close Communist allies after 1949, bound by ideology and a 1950 mutual defense treaty.
trajectory: Ideological divergence (de-Stalinization, competing visions of communism) and border disputes turned allies into rivals within about a decade, including a 1969 border war.
outcome: Full rupture of the alliance, which later enabled the US-China rapprochement (see that case) as China sought a counterweight to the USSR.
key_lesson: Alliances built on ideology rather than mutual material interest can rupture quickly once ideological interpretation diverges, and the rupture can reshape the entire global balance of power.

name: South Africa's international isolation and transition
initial_dynamic: Apartheid regime faced growing international condemnation starting in the 1960s.
trajectory: Escalating sanctions and divestment campaigns through the 1970s-80s (UN arms embargo, US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act 1986) increased economic pressure without a single trigger event; internal resistance grew in parallel.
outcome: Sustained multilateral pressure combined with internal political change led to negotiated transition and free elections in 1994 — a case where sanctions pressure is generally credited as a significant contributing factor.
key_lesson: Sustained multilateral economic pressure can contribute meaningfully to political change, but usually only works over long timeframes (decades) and in combination with internal political shifts, not as a fast lever on its own.

name: US-Mexico from war to economic integration
initial_dynamic: Mexican-American War (1846-48) resulted in Mexico losing roughly half its territory; deep historical grievance.
trajectory: Relations normalized over the following century, then deepened dramatically through economic integration (NAFTA 1994, USMCA 2020), even as periodic friction (immigration, drug trafficking, tariff threats) continued.
outcome: From territorial war to one of the most economically integrated bilateral relationships in the world, though political friction never fully disappeared.
key_lesson: Deep economic integration can coexist with — and outlast — significant unresolved political friction; the two don't have to resolve together.

name: Concert of Europe
initial_dynamic: Great powers exhausted by the Napoleonic Wars sought to prevent another continent-wide conflict.
trajectory: A deliberate system of regular diplomatic congresses to manage disputes and maintain a balance of power among rivals, rather than letting rivalries escalate unchecked.
outcome: Produced roughly four decades of relative great-power peace in Europe (no general war until Crimea in 1853) — an unusually long stretch for that era.
key_lesson: Institutionalized, regular diplomatic management of rivalry (not resolving the rivalry, just managing it) can suppress escalation for a long time, even among powers with real conflicting interests.

name: Greece-Turkey Aegean and Cyprus disputes
initial_dynamic: NATO allies with overlapping claims (Aegean airspace/waters, Cyprus) that have brought them to the brink of war multiple times despite the alliance.
trajectory: Repeated crisis-and-thaw cycles (near-war in 1996, 'earthquake diplomacy' thaw in 1999, renewed tension in the 2020s over energy exploration rights) with no permanent resolution.
outcome: Persistent low-grade rivalry contained by NATO membership and mutual deterrence, never fully resolved despite 50 years of intermittent talks.
key_lesson: Shared alliance membership can cap escalation (prevent full war) without ever resolving the underlying dispute — expect indefinite oscillation, not a clean endpoint.

name: UK-Argentina Falklands War
initial_dynamic: Long-standing but low-intensity territorial dispute over the Falkland Islands.
trajectory: Argentina's military junta invaded in April 1982, likely partly to rally domestic support amid economic crisis; the UK responded with a full military campaign and retook the islands within ten weeks.
outcome: Decisive military resolution in the UK's favor; the junta collapsed shortly after defeat, but the underlying territorial dispute remains formally unresolved to this day (Argentina still claims the islands).
key_lesson: A domestically-motivated gamble by a weaker/more desperate party can trigger a short sharp conflict that resolves the immediate crisis militarily while leaving the root dispute permanently unsettled.

name: China-Vietnam war and normalization
initial_dynamic: Former allies against the US turned hostile after Vietnam's 1978 invasion of Cambodia (ousting a Chinese-backed regime) and mistreatment of ethnic Chinese in Vietnam.
trajectory: China launched a brief punitive invasion in 1979 (both sides claimed victory, neither achieved decisive goals); a decade of border skirmishes and hostility followed.
outcome: Full diplomatic normalization in 1991 once the Cold War context that drove the split (competing Soviet/Chinese patronage) faded.
key_lesson: Rivalries between former allies that were really driven by a third party's influence (here, Sino-Soviet competition for Vietnam) tend to fade once that third-party dynamic resolves, even after a war.

name: US-Cuba relations
initial_dynamic: Cuban Revolution (1959) and subsequent alignment with the USSR led to a US embargo and near-nuclear-war crisis (1962 Missile Crisis).
trajectory: Over 50 years of embargo and estrangement, followed by a dramatic thaw under Obama (2014-2016 normalization, embassy reopenings), which then partially reversed under the following administration.
outcome: Long-frozen relationship saw one major breakthrough that proved only partially durable — subsequent policy reversed much of the opening.
key_lesson: Even a serious, high-profile normalization effort after a very long freeze can be substantially unwound by a change in the initiating country's domestic politics — durability depends on institutionalizing the thaw beyond one administration.
